summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in Côte d'Ivoire and have never been criminalized.

Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes public breach of decency with three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent or contrary-to-nature act with an individual of the same sex, the penalty is six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled if committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor of eighteen years.

Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for homosexual couples and 15 for heterosexual couples.

Côte d'Ivoire provides no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. No legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation exists either.

The government does not recognize same-sex couples.

The United States Department of State 2023 report on human rights practices records three deaths within the LGBTQI+ community during that year. In the same year a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Police responses to such non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years. Many victims do not report to police because they believe they will not be taken seriously.

In September and October 2024, 45 assault incidents were recorded in Abidjan. Social media influencers called for violence during that period. A homophobia-motivated attack occurred at a market employing gay hair stylists. After these attacks people avoided going out during the day and meeting publicly and remained hypervigilant.

Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face an especially high risk of violence because their gender expression breaks social norms and draws hostile attention. Peer-reviewed research published in 2015 found that travestis, people born anatomically male who live as women, face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention.

During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, the Force Républicaines de Côte d’Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers. Complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals. Fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis, defined as transgender and otherwise gender non-conforming people assigned male at birth. In 2012 members of the same force repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar in Abidjan frequented by gender and sexual minorities, mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes forcing them to remove clothes, and demanding a significant fine under threat of being taken to bases.

In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis, gay men and trans women, and lelés, lesbians and trans men, stating that despite their different sexual orientation and contrary to customs and traditions, members of this woubi community remain human beings and benefit from human rights enshrined in the Ivorian Constitution and international human rights treaties. In 2024 President Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to counter the expansion of homosexuality.

Discrimination in healthcare continues, including refusal of care on grounds of sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Sexual minorities, transgender and gender non-conforming people are seen as abnormal and their identities are perceived as stemming from the Global North.

Misinformation circulated during the 2024 wave of attacks, including a hoax that the French President had asked the Ivorian President to legalize same-sex marriage.

Wealthier people are treated with less hostility than poorer people.

A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preach against the community.

In March 2010 the Ivorian representative stated the country would begin to take measures to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, but would not start awareness-raising programs because it was not a current priority.
localsOnly:
Many transgender people lack secure housing. Evictions and family expulsions have caused school dropout.

Discrimination continues in housing and employment, including refusal to hire or promote or firing if sexual orientation or gender identity is discovered.

Reported conversion practices in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend a prayer camp.

Gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognized as eligible to adopt.

The 2015 research found travestis were underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them and examined their isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

A doctor refused service a few years before September 2011 because of sexual orientation, until protest led to care being provided.
outOfScopeNotes:
Placement of transgender detainees is unresolved. No listed Human Rights Watch publication for Côte d'Ivoire documents whether placement is by birth sex or identity, whether dedicated units exist, or whether solitary confinement or segregation is used. On the Human Rights Watch country page, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

Detention conditions beyond the absence noted above are not sourced in the inventory.
